quiz.q: A tracheostomy patient becomes obstructed and desaturates. Where is oxygen applied?
choices: Over the mouth and nose with a non-rebreather
At the tracheostomy stoma
By nasal cannula at 6 L/min
Nowhere until the tube is replaced
quiz.why: A tracheostomy bypasses the upper airway, so a mask over the face delivers oxygen to a route that is not connected to the lungs. Oxygen goes to the stoma, and delaying oxygen entirely is never correct.

quiz.q: What is the correct wall suction setting for a 4-year-old?
choices: 80 to 120 mmHg
60 to 100 mmHg
100 to 150 mmHg
150 to 200 mmHg
quiz.why: Children are suctioned at 80 to 120 mmHg. Sixty to 100 is the infant and neonate range, 100 to 150 is adult, and anything above 150 tears pediatric mucosa without clearing secretions better.

quiz.q: During trach suctioning a colleague instills 5 mL of saline down the tube to loosen secretions. What is the current guidance?
choices: Correct technique for thick secretions
Acceptable if the patient is preoxygenated
Not recommended — it pushes bacteria toward the lungs without reliably thinning secretions
Required before every suction pass
quiz.why: Routine saline instillation has been abandoned because it dislodges biofilm into the lower airway and worsens desaturation without improving secretion clearance. Preoxygenation does not change that.

quiz.q: You are bagging a patient and the chest rises but the abdomen is visibly distending. What is happening?
choices: Normal with a bag-valve-mask
The reservoir bag is not attached
The oxygen flow is set too low
Ventilations are too fast or too forceful and gas is entering the stomach
quiz.why: Gastric insufflation results from pressure exceeding esophageal opening pressure, caused by rapid or forceful squeezing. Slow to about 1 second per breath with only enough volume for chest rise. Reservoir and flow affect FiO2, not insufflation.

quiz.q: A drowsy patient gags when you attempt to place an oral airway. What is the correct device?
choices: Insert the OPA anyway to protect the airway
A nasopharyngeal airway, sized nostril to earlobe and lubricated
A larger OPA, which will pass more easily
No adjunct; reposition the head only
quiz.why: An intact gag reflex contraindicates an OPA because it induces vomiting. An NPA is tolerated with an intact gag. A larger OPA worsens the problem, and repositioning alone may not maintain patency.

quiz.q: Which item is NOT part of building an intubation setup?
choices: A tube one size smaller than requested
A supraglottic rescue airway
Programming the sedation infusion pump
Waveform capnography connected and ready
quiz.why: Techs do not program pumps; that is a nursing function. The backup tube, a rescue airway and ready capnography are all standard components of the tray a tech builds.

quiz.q: You are handed the endotracheal tube to hold immediately after placement. What is your responsibility?
choices: Hold it exactly at the depth given and do not let it move until it is secured
Secure it with tape yourself as fast as possible
Release it once capnography confirms placement
Advance it 2 cm for a safety margin
quiz.why: Any movement can displace the tube into the right mainstem bronchus or out of the trachea entirely. You hold the depth and report the centimeter marking. Advancing it is never your decision.

quiz.q: A firefighter rescued from a structure fire has an SpO2 of 100% on room air and a headache. What should you understand about the reading?
choices: It rules out significant hypoxia and carbon monoxide exposure
It confirms the probe is on the wrong finger
It means the patient is hyperventilating
It may be falsely normal because carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light like oxyhemoglobin
quiz.why: A standard pulse oximeter cannot distinguish carbon monoxide-bound from oxygen-bound hemoglobin. A high reading in a fire victim with a headache is a red flag requiring co-oximetry, not reassurance.

quiz.q: A large-armed patient's automated blood pressure reads 190/110 on a regular adult cuff. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Report a hypertensive emergency immediately
Repeat with a correctly sized large cuff before anyone acts on the number
Repeat on the same arm three times and average
Move the cuff to the forearm and use that reading
quiz.why: An undersized cuff reads falsely high. Averaging three wrong readings does not fix the error, a forearm reading is not equivalent to an upper arm reading, and treating an artifact as an emergency leads to unnecessary intervention.

quiz.q: A monitor shows a wandering, noisy baseline on lead II. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A dried-out or poorly adhered electrode
The patient is in ventricular fibrillation
The monitor needs to be replaced
The alarm limits are set incorrectly
quiz.why: Dry gel, poor skin prep, hair and loose wires produce baseline wander. VF has a coarse chaotic pattern with a clinically arrested patient. Alarm limits do not affect the tracing quality and replacing the monitor skips the obvious fix.

quiz.q: An IV site is red, warm, painful, and a firm cord is palpable along the vein. What is this?
choices: Infiltration
Extravasation of a vesicant
Normal after 12 hours of infusion
Phlebitis
quiz.why: Redness, warmth, pain and a palpable cord describe vein inflammation. Infiltration is cool, swollen and blanched. Extravasation involves a tissue-damaging drug leaking out and causes blistering or necrosis. None of this is normal.

quiz.q: An infusion pump alarms 'air in line' during transport. What does a tech do?
choices: Clear the alarm and continue
Prime the line to remove the air
Stop and notify the nurse without clearing the alarm
Disconnect the line from the IV catheter
quiz.why: Techs do not clear infusion alarms, prime lines or disconnect infusions. All three are medication administration functions. Reporting preserves the alarm state the nurse needs to assess.

quiz.q: How should a pulse oximeter probe and a blood pressure cuff be positioned relative to each other?
choices: On the same arm, so the other arm is free for IV access
On opposite limbs, because a cycling cuff cuts off the pulsatile signal
Either way; the cuff does not affect the probe
Both on the same arm but with the probe on the thumb
quiz.why: Cuff inflation occludes arterial flow distal to it, so the oximeter loses its signal or reads falsely low with every cycle. Digit choice does not fix this. Opposite limbs is the rule.

quiz.q: You are taking a patient down a ramp in a wheelchair. Which approach is correct?
choices: Backward, with you descending ahead of the chair
Forward, moving slowly
Forward with the footrests removed
Sideways, angled across the slope
quiz.why: Descending backward keeps the patient from pitching forward and puts your body between the chair and the downhill. Forward travel relies on the patient's balance, and crossing a slope invites a lateral tip.

quiz.q: A 480-pound patient needs to go to CT. What is the first thing to establish?
choices: Whether enough staff are available to lift manually
Whether the patient can walk there
Which technologist is on duty
The weight rating of the stretcher, the CT table and the route
quiz.why: Equipment ratings determine whether the move is possible at all, and exceeding one causes catastrophic failure. Manual lifting at this weight is unsafe regardless of staffing, and ambulation does not solve the table limit.

quiz.q: Which practice with a full-body mechanical lift is correct?
choices: One trained staff member may operate it alone
The patient may be left suspended briefly while the chair is positioned
Two staff minimum, sling inspected for frayed stitching, patient never left suspended
The sling rating does not matter if the lift is rated appropriately
quiz.why: Two staff, an inspected sling of the correct rating, and continuous attendance are the standard. A sling is a separate rated component and is the part that actually fails. Suspending a patient unattended is how they are dropped.

quiz.q: A trauma patient arrives cold and wet after an extrication. Why does warming matter beyond comfort?
choices: Warm patients report less pain
Hypothermia impairs clotting and is part of the trauma triad of death
Warming raises blood pressure directly
Cold skin makes IV access impossible
quiz.why: Clotting factor function falls sharply with temperature, so a cold bleeding patient keeps bleeding. Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy reinforce each other. Comfort and access are real but secondary considerations.

quiz.q: A tech tucks a forced-air warmer hose under a blanket without attaching the disposable warming blanket. What is the outcome risk?
choices: Deep thermal burns to the skin
Inadequate warming with no direct harm
Contamination of the warming unit
Excessive humidification of the bedding
quiz.why: Free-hosing concentrates high-temperature air on a small skin area and causes full-thickness burns. It is a recognized never-event, not merely an ineffective technique.

quiz.q: During targeted temperature management after cardiac arrest, the patient begins shivering. Why does this matter?
choices: Shivering indicates the patient is waking up and cooling should stop
Shivering is expected and requires no action
Shivering means the surface pads are too tight
Shivering generates heat and defeats cooling, so it is reported immediately
quiz.why: Muscle activity produces heat and raises oxygen consumption, working directly against the target temperature. It requires treatment, which is why it is escalated. It is not a reliable sign of neurologic recovery.

quiz.q: You scan a post-hysterectomy woman's bladder on the female setting and get 180 mL. What is the concern?
choices: The volume is accurate and no action is needed
The female algorithm subtracts a uterus she does not have, so the true volume is higher
The probe was aimed too high
Bladder scanners cannot be used after abdominal surgery
quiz.why: The female setting applies a uterine correction that falsely lowers the reading in a patient without a uterus. The correct choice is the male setting. Aiming and surgical history are separate issues, and scanners are usable after remote surgery.

quiz.q: A patient has not voided in eight hours. A bladder scan reads 520 mL. How should you report it?
choices: "Bladder scan 520 mL, no void in eight hours, patient reports suprapubic discomfort."
"Bladder scan is high."
"Patient probably needs a catheter."
"Scan was inconclusive."
quiz.why: A number plus the relevant context is what a nurse can act on. Vague adjectives, a recommendation for a procedure you do not order, and a false claim of inconclusiveness all obscure the finding.

quiz.q: You find a crash cart whose plastic lock number does not match the number on the log. What is required?
choices: Correct the number on the log and sign it
Replace the lock with one matching the log
Fully inventory and restock the cart, then reseal with a new number and record it
Take the cart out of service permanently
quiz.why: A mismatch means the seal was broken and the contents cannot be assumed complete. Editing the log or reapplying a lock to unverified contents falsifies the check. Permanent removal is unnecessary once the cart is restocked.

quiz.q: During a defibrillator check you find the unit passes its self-test but is not plugged into wall power. What does this mean?
choices: It is fine as long as the battery shows charge
The self-test result is invalid
The pads must be replaced
The unit is running down its battery and must be plugged in — battery-only readiness is not acceptable
quiz.why: A defibrillator left unplugged drains toward a dead battery at the worst possible moment. Wall power is a required element of the check. The self-test result stands, and pads are a separate check item.

quiz.q: A tech restocks a supply cabinet by placing the newly delivered boxes in front of the existing ones. What is the error?
choices: Nothing; newer stock is preferable
Stock rotation is reversed — new stock goes behind old so the nearest expiration is used first
Par levels have been exceeded
The cabinet should be restocked only by materials management
quiz.why: First in, first out is what prevents expired supplies accumulating at the back. The par level is about quantity, not arrangement, and restocking rooms is a core tech function.

quiz.q: A wheelchair has a cracked footrest bracket. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Leave it in the hallway and warn coworkers
Use it carefully without the footrest until a replacement arrives
Tag it out of service with the date and defect, remove it to biomedical engineering, enter a work order, and bring a working replacement
Repair it yourself with tape
quiz.why: Tag, remove, report, replace. Leaving a defective device accessible guarantees someone grabs it in a hurry, continued use risks injury, and improvised repairs on patient equipment are never acceptable.

quiz.q: A patient is injured when a warming device malfunctions. What must happen to the device?
choices: Clean and return it to service after confirming it now works
Send it immediately to biomedical engineering for repair
Sequester it unchanged with its disposables and packaging, record the settings, and notify the charge nurse
Discard it and document the model number
quiz.why: The device and its settings are evidence under medical device reporting requirements. Cleaning, resetting, repairing or discarding it destroys the data needed to determine the cause and to report it to the manufacturer and the FDA.

scenarios.title: Room 6: 68-year-old COPD, working hard
scenarios.intro:
Mr. Whelan, 68, arrived by car with three days of worsening shortness of breath. He has severe COPD, smokes, and uses home oxygen at 2 L. He is sitting forward on the edge of the stretcher, speaking in three-word sentences, with pursed lips and visible accessory muscle use.

The nurse is starting an IV and calls to you: "Get him on oxygen and set up a neb — DuoNeb is ordered. And call respiratory."

steps.prompt: Room air saturation on the portable probe is 84%. He has known COPD. What do you set up?

choices.text: Start controlled oxygen aiming for the 88 to 92% COPD target, tell the nurse the room air saturation, and set up the nebulizer
choices.feedback: Right. Eighty-four percent needs treatment, and the target is 88 to 92% rather than 100%. You report the room air number because it is the baseline everything else is compared to.

choices.text: Place a non-rebreather at 15 L/min immediately to get him to 100%
choices.feedback: Overshooting. He is hypoxic and does need oxygen, but driving a chronic retainer to 100% can worsen CO2 retention. Titrate to 88 to 92% and tell the nurse.

choices.text: Leave him on room air since 84% is his baseline with COPD and set up the neb only
choices.feedback: Harmful. Eighty-four percent is below the COPD target of 88 to 92%. Assuming a number is someone's baseline without data is how hypoxia gets missed.

choices.text: Set up the nebulizer first and add oxygen once respiratory therapy arrives
choices.feedback: Too slow, and unnecessary — the nebulizer itself can be driven with oxygen. He needs supplemental oxygen now, not after someone else arrives.

steps.prompt: You are setting up the DuoNeb. The order says to drive it with oxygen. What flow do you set, and how do you position him?

choices.text: 6 to 8 L/min on the green outlet, patient sitting fully upright, and tell him to breathe normally with an occasional deep breath
choices.feedback: Exactly right. Six to eight liters produces respirable particle size, upright maximizes deposition, and normal tidal breathing works better than forced fast inhalation.

choices.text: 3 L/min so the mist is gentler and he tolerates it
choices.feedback: Harmful. Below 6 L/min the droplets are too large to reach the small airways. You would run a 20-minute treatment that delivers almost nothing to the lungs.

choices.text: 8 L/min on the yellow outlet, since air drives a nebulizer fine
choices.feedback: The flow is right but the gas is wrong for this patient. He is at 84% — the order says oxygen. Medical air would drive the neb and leave him hypoxic throughout.

choices.text: 8 L/min with the patient reclined at 30 degrees so he can rest during the treatment
choices.feedback: The flow is correct. The position is not — a patient slumped back deposits most of the drug in the mouth, and a COPD patient in distress needs to sit forward anyway.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes later the treatment is done. He is still working hard. Respiratory therapy arrives and says BiPAP. The RT asks you to get the machine and a mask.

choices.text: Bring the machine and circuit, size a full-face mask from the nose bridge to just below the lower lip, and get suction set up at the head of the bed
choices.feedback: Complete. Correct sizing plus suction ready is exactly what the RT needs from you — the mask has to come off fast if he vomits.

choices.text: Bring the machine and grab the largest mask so there is no chance of a leak
choices.feedback: Backwards. An oversized mask leaks more, not less, because it cannot seal on the face contours. Size it with the gauge.

choices.text: Bring the machine and mask and set the IPAP and EPAP to the usual starting numbers to save time
choices.feedback: Out of scope. Pressures are set by respiratory therapy or the physician. Setting them yourself is medication-level decision-making with a machine.

choices.text: Bring the machine and a correctly sized mask, and go find suction after the RT has him started
choices.feedback: The mask is right. Suction after the fact is too late — if he vomits into a strapped-on mask in the first two minutes, you need it already there.

steps.prompt: The RT is ready to apply the mask. Mr. Whelan is anxious and pulling at it. The RT asks you to help with the fit.

choices.text: Hold the mask gently on his face for the first minute while talking him through it, then strap it two fingers loose with a foam dressing on the nasal bridge
choices.feedback: This is the technique that makes NIV succeed. Most failures happen in the first sixty seconds when a panicked patient has a mask strapped down. Holding it first lets him acclimate.

choices.text: Strap it down firmly right away so he cannot pull it off and gets the pressure immediately
choices.feedback: This is how NIV fails. A strapped-on mask on a panicking patient produces fighting, worse work of breathing, and a nasal bridge ulcer. He also removes it the moment you step away.

choices.text: Hold the mask on his face but tighten the straps hard once he settles, to eliminate any leak
choices.feedback: The first half is right. Over-tightening deforms the cushion and usually creates more leak, plus it causes pressure injury on the bridge within hours. Two fingers of slack.

choices.text: Tell him to calm down and hold still, and apply the mask
choices.feedback: Telling an air-hungry person to calm down does nothing and costs you trust. Coach him through what the pressure will feel like while you hold the mask.

steps.prompt: Thirty-five minutes on BiPAP. He was fighting the mask; now he is quiet and slow to respond when you say his name. His saturation is 93%.

choices.text: Get the nurse and the RT now — new drowsiness on BiPAP suggests rising CO2, and report the level of consciousness change specifically
choices.feedback: Correct and urgent. The saturation improved, which is exactly what makes this dangerous — the number looks better while the patient is failing. Somnolence on NIV is the deterioration sign.

choices.text: Note that his respiratory rate came down and his saturation improved, and chart that he is tolerating BiPAP well
choices.feedback: This is the trap. A falling respiratory rate with rising sedation is not improvement — it is a patient tiring out or retaining CO2. The numbers look good right up until he stops breathing.

choices.text: Lower the FiO2 since the saturation is above the COPD target
choices.feedback: Adjusting settings is not yours to do, and the urgent issue is the mental status change, not the saturation. Report it.

choices.text: Try to wake him and recheck in ten minutes
choices.feedback: Checking is better than nothing, but ten minutes is a long time in impending respiratory failure. This is a now conversation with the nurse and the RT.

scenarios.debrief:
Two patterns worth carrying.

First, **the COPD oxygen target is 88 to 92%, and both errors are real.** Leaving him at 84% because "he's a COPD patient" is hypoxia. Slamming him to 100% is CO2 retention. The device you set up and the flow you choose are how you land in between, and every report carries the device and the flow, not just the number.

Second, **nebulizer flow is a therapeutic dose.** Turning it down to 3 L/min because the patient dislikes the mist converts a bronchodilator treatment into twenty minutes of nothing. Six to eight liters, upright, tidal breathing.

And the one that kills people: **improving numbers with a deteriorating patient.** His respiratory rate fell from 32 to 18 and his saturation rose to 93%, and he was getting worse. Somnolence on noninvasive ventilation is rising carbon dioxide until proven otherwise. Report the mental status, not the monitor.

scenarios.title: 0700: the cart check nobody wants to do
scenarios.intro:
You are the day tech in the resuscitation area. The department was busy overnight — two codes and a trauma. Your first tasks are the crash cart check, the resus bay restock, and getting bay 1 ready in case anything rolls in.

The cart log on the clipboard has a signature for yesterday day shift and nothing since. The night tech is already gone.

steps.prompt: You look at the cart. The plastic breakaway lock is intact but the number reads 4471. The log's last entry lists lock number 4468. What does that tell you, and what do you do?

choices.text: The cart was opened and resealed without being logged — inventory the entire cart, restock it, reseal with a new lock, and record both the number and the discrepancy
choices.feedback: Right. An intact lock only means something if the number matches a documented check. A changed number with no log entry means you cannot assume the contents are complete.

choices.text: The lock is intact, so the cart is complete — sign the log with the new number
choices.feedback: Harmful. You would be certifying contents nobody verified. Someone opened it during a code and resealed it; whether it was restocked is unknown.

choices.text: Write 4471 over 4468 on the log to correct the record and move on
choices.feedback: That is falsifying a safety record. The discrepancy is the finding — it gets documented, not erased.

choices.text: Leave it and ask the charge nurse whether the night shift restocked it
choices.feedback: Asking is reasonable, but the answer does not change what you have to do. A number mismatch with no log entry means the cart gets inventoried regardless of what anyone remembers.

steps.prompt: You inventory the cart. Everything is present except the amiodarone, which is short by one box, and a bag of pediatric IO needles that were used. You move on to the defibrillator. It powers on, passes its self-test, shows a full battery icon, and the pads are sealed. The power cord is coiled on the shelf, unplugged.

choices.text: Replace the missing items, plug the defibrillator into wall power, verify the pad expiration dates, and check the paper roll
choices.feedback: All four. An unplugged defibrillator is running down its battery toward the worst possible moment, and 'pads present and sealed' is not the same as 'pads in date'.

choices.text: Note the self-test passed and the battery is full, and move on — it will hold charge for the shift
choices.feedback: Harmful. Wall power is a required element of the check, not an optional one. A battery that reads full at 0700 is not a plan for a code at 1800.

choices.text: Plug it in and restock the cart, but skip the pad dates since the packages are sealed
choices.feedback: Half right. Sealed packaging says nothing about the expiration date, and expired pads have degraded gel that will not conduct. Dates are checked on every cart check.

choices.text: Take the defibrillator out of service because the cart had missing items
choices.feedback: Disproportionate. The missing supplies are a restock issue, not a defibrillator fault. Removing the only defibrillator in the resus bay creates a far bigger hazard.

steps.prompt: Bay 1 next. The suction canister is a third full from last night, the oxygen E cylinder on the stretcher reads 400 psi, and the wall suction regulator is set but has no Yankauer attached.

choices.text: Swap the cylinder for a full one, attach a Yankauer, set the regulator to 100 to 150 mmHg, occlude the tubing to confirm it pulls, and change the canister
choices.feedback: This is what 'suction is set up' actually means. Four hundred psi is below the 500 threshold, and a regulator without a tip on it is a box on a wall.

choices.text: Leave the 400 psi cylinder since the bay has wall oxygen anyway, and attach a Yankauer
choices.feedback: The Yankauer is right. The tank is not — the moment that patient goes to CT, 400 psi is what they travel on. Swap anything under 500.

choices.text: Attach the Yankauer and set the regulator to 200 mmHg so it clears thick vomit faster
choices.feedback: Higher pressure does not clear thick material better; it tears mucosa and strips more oxygen. Adult wall suction is 100 to 150 mmHg.

choices.text: Swap the cylinder and attach a Yankauer, but leave the canister since it is only a third full
choices.feedback: Reasonable on the canister — two-thirds to three-quarters is the change threshold. But last night's contents in a fresh bay is sloppy, and it costs thirty seconds to start clean.

steps.prompt: Restocking the bay, you find the sharps container is at the fill line and the top drawer's IV start kits are two deep with a delivery box of new ones sitting on the counter. You also notice one of the two infusion pumps in the bay has a cracked housing and a frayed power cord.

choices.text: Replace the sharps container, put the new IV kits behind the existing ones, and tag the pump out of service, remove it to biomed, enter a work order and bring a replacement
choices.feedback: Every piece correct. Sharps go at the fill line, not when jammed; stock rotates first in first out; and a frayed cord is an electrical hazard that leaves the department.

choices.text: Replace the sharps container, stack the new kits in front for easy reach, and set the cracked pump aside in the hallway with a note
choices.feedback: Two errors. New stock in front means the old ones expire at the back, and a broken pump in a hallway gets grabbed during the next emergency no matter what the note says.

choices.text: Leave the sharps container since a few more will fit, rotate the kits correctly, and tag the pump
choices.feedback: The rotation and the tag are right. Pushing more into a container at the fill line is exactly how needlesticks happen — that is the trigger to change it.

choices.text: Wrap the frayed cord in tape, rotate the stock, and change the sharps container
choices.feedback: Taping a damaged power cord on patient equipment is not a repair. A frayed three-prong cord is a shock and fire hazard and the device leaves the floor.

steps.prompt: It is 0740. Everything is done. What goes on paper, and what goes to the charge nurse?

choices.text: Sign and time the cart log noting the lock discrepancy, the full inventory and the new lock number; enter the pump work order; and tell the charge nurse the cart was opened overnight without a log entry
choices.feedback: Complete. The signature with a time is what makes the check real, the discrepancy is a safety finding that belongs in front of a leader, and the work order is what actually gets the pump fixed.

choices.text: Sign the cart log and mention the pump verbally at huddle
choices.feedback: Partial. A verbal mention without a work order means the pump sits in biomed unlogged, and an unnoted lock discrepancy means the pattern never gets addressed.

choices.text: Sign the log with the new lock number and say nothing about the discrepancy, since you restocked it
choices.feedback: Fixing it is not the same as reporting it. A cart opened during a code and left unlogged is a process failure that will repeat, and the next tech may not catch it.

choices.text: Leave the log for the charge nurse to sign since she is responsible for the cart
choices.feedback: You did the check; you sign it. An unsigned log is treated as a check that did not happen, and handing it off breaks the accountability the log exists to create.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern is that **equipment readiness is a documentation task as much as a physical one.** An intact lock proves nothing unless its number matches a signed log. A defibrillator that passes its self-test is still a failure waiting to happen if it is unplugged. A regulator with the pressure set is not suction until a Yankauer is on it and you have watched it pull.

The numbers to carry out of this: adult wall suction `100 to 150 mmHg`; swap any E cylinder under `500 psi`; change a sharps container at the fill line, roughly three-quarters; change a suction canister at two-thirds to three-quarters; rotate stock first in, first out with new behind old.

And the professional habit underneath all of it: **tag, remove, report, replace** for anything broken, and report the process failure, not just the item. Fixing a problem quietly means the next person meets it again.
